extracted.intended_audience: recipients of Federal financial assistance (K-12 and higher education institutions), Title IX coordinators, school administrators, institutional legal counsel, and policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how schools and institutions must structure and carry out Title IX grievance processes, interact with State/local laws, and provide supportive measures, advisors, and remedies consistent with final Title IX regulations (notably §§106.30, 106.44, 106.45, and §106.6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemption of conflicting State/local law (§106.6(h))
rubrics_metrics.description: To the extent of a conflict between State or local law and Title IX as implemented by §§ 106.30, 106.44, and 106.45, the obligation to comply with §§ 106.30, 106.44, and 106.45 is not obviated or alleviated by any State or local law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the event of an actual conflict, the final regulations have preemptive effect over conflicting State or local law. The Department added §106.6(h) to make this clear and to address commenters' questions about preemption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prompt response when institution has actual knowledge (§106.44(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient must respond “promptly” when it has actual knowledge of sexual harassment in its education program or activity pursuant to § 106.44(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prompt response is required even where temporary delays for good cause (e.g., concurrent law enforcement activity) occur; any allowed delay must still be consistent with the obligation to respond promptly overall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonably prompt time frames to conclude grievance process (§106.45(b)(1)(v))
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 106.45(b)(1)(v) requires reasonably prompt time frames for the conclusion of the grievance process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requirement does not inherently conflict with State laws that permit temporary delays for good cause (for example, a 10‑day law‑enforcement delay) so long as the recipient responds promptly when it has actual knowledge and meets the reasonably prompt conclusion timeframes it has designated.

rubrics_metrics.name: No required single definition of consent (§106.30)
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.30 expressly states that the Assistant Secretary will not require recipients to adopt a particular definition of consent with respect to sexual assault.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients and States remain free to adopt their own definitions of consent (for example, affirmative consent) without conflicting with these final regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory dismissal is only for Title IX purposes (§106.45(b)(3)(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: A mandatory dismissal of allegations in a formal complaint of sexual harassment because the allegations concern sexual harassment that occurred outside the United States (or otherwise fall outside Title IX) is a dismissal only for Title IX purposes and does not preclude action under another provision of the recipient's code of conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients may pursue disciplinary or remedial action under their own policies or State law even when the conduct is dismissed for Title IX purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parties may have an advisor of choice, including union representative (§106.45(b)(2)(i)(B) and §106.45(b)(5)(iv))
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must provide written notice that the parties may have 'an advisor of their choice, who may be, but is not required to be, an attorney' and must provide parties with the same opportunities to have an advisor present during any grievance proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nothing in the final regulations precludes a party from selecting a union representative as their advisor of choice. If State law requires a union representative be present for investigatory interviews, permitting that presence is not inherently in conflict with these regulations, unless an actual conflict exists; §106.6(h) governs preemption in those cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality of party identities with statutory exceptions (§106.71)
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.71 requires a recipient to keep confidential the identity of parties to a Title IX grievance process, except as required by law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This confidentiality limitation may constrain permitting persons other than a party's advisor to be present during proceedings, but recipients must follow any legal exceptions (e.g., State law that requires certain representation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of decision‑maker from investigator/Title IX Coordinator (§106.45(b)(7)(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations preclude the decision‑maker from being the same person as the Title IX Coordinator or the investigator, though they do not preclude the Title IX Coordinator from also serving as the investigator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The investigator may make recommendations in an investigative report, but the decision‑maker must exercise independent judgment and objectively evaluate relevant evidence to reach a determination regarding responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdictional limitation to persons in the United States and education program/activity (20 U.S.C. 1681(a) / §106.8(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations recognize the jurisdictional limitation in the Title IX statute (20 U.S.C. 1681(a))—that Title IX applies where conduct affects 'no person in the United States'—and accordingly a mandatory dismissal may occur when allegations concern conduct outside the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This limitation does not prevent recipients from addressing conduct that occurs outside the United States pursuant to their own codes of conduct or State law (e.g., disciplinary action in study abroad contexts); §106.45(b)(3)(i) was revised to clarify the dismissal is Title IX‑only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients may adopt and apply State/local laws that are more protective or broader
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing in the final regulations prevents recipients from initiating student conduct proceedings, offering supportive measures, or otherwise responding to conduct outside Title IX scope; recipients are free to comply with State laws that require broader definitions or additional coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where State law imposes stricter reporting requirements, broader definitions of sexual harassment, or requirements to address off‑campus conduct, recipients may comply with those State requirements so long as they also comply with Title IX obligations; such complementarities do not inherently create conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supportive measures and equitable treatment (§106.44(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.44(a) requires a recipient to treat complainants and respondents equitably by offering supportive measures (as defined in §106.30) to a complainant and by following a §106.45‑compliant grievance process before imposing disciplinary sanctions or other actions that are not supportive measures against a respondent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supportive measures are designed to restore or preserve equal access to the education program or activity without unreasonably burdening the other party. If a respondent is found responsible, the recipient must effectively implement remedies designed to restore or preserve equal access (§106.45(b)(1)(i); §106.45(b)(7)(iv)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence standard flexibility (preponderance permitted)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients are free to adopt the preponderance of the evidence standard; the Department disagrees that the final regulations conflict with State laws that require preponderance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using the same standard for complaints against employees and students is allowed and may address power‑differential concerns; if State law requires preponderance, applying that standard does not conflict with these regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross‑examination conducted by advisors; direct party questioning prohibited (§106.45(b)(6)(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations do not require parties to directly cross‑examine each other; instead, cross‑examination is conducted by a party's advisor and personal questioning by one party of another is expressly prohibited under §106.45(b)(6)(i).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach may differ from State practices (for example, where a State prohibits cross‑examination entirely or allows only indirect questioning), but the regulations require advisor‑conducted cross‑examination as part of the grievance process. Recipients must balance this requirement with any applicable legal constraints and preemption guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal opportunity to inspect and review evidence; documentation sharing
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations contemplate providing documentation and opportunities to inspect and review evidence to both parties as part of the grievance process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concerns that this conflicts with certain court practices (e.g., restrictions on providing police reports to complainants) were addressed: the regulations do not appear to conflict with such court practices because those practices do not necessarily mandate institutional procedures; recipients should follow applicable law while providing required opportunities under §106.45.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights of minors and reliance on State/local practice (§106.6(g))
rubrics_metrics.description: When a party is a minor, has a guardian, is attending elementary/secondary school, or is under age 18, recipients have discretion to look to State law and local educational practice in determining whether rights shall be exercised by the parent(s) or guardian(s) instead of or in addition to the party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The NPRM acknowledged this and the final regulations set forth the proposition more clearly in §106.6(g), giving recipients flexibility in exercising minors' rights consistent with State/local practice.
